headline: Captree dock talk: bass gone to the night shift, fluke still paying the bills
subhead: Warm water pushed the stripers deep and nocturnal, but the inlet's still handing out keeper fluke and the blues never left.
body_markdown:
Guy pulls up to the scale Tuesday morning with a cooler half-empty and a face like he lost a bet. "Mari, where'd all the bass go? I fished the Robert Moses bridge for two hours on the last of the ebb, nothing but blowfish and a couple rat blues." I didn't even have to look at the thermometer to answer him — I already knew. Water's sitting in the low-to-mid 70s off the beach and inside the bay, and when it gets that warm on top, the bass do what they always do this time of year: they go down and they go dark. Literally. Daytime bite on stripers right now is a coin flip at best. Nighttime, working bunker chunks or eels around the deeper holes off Democrat Point and the west end of the inlet, that's where the real fish are living.

We called this one a few days back — said the surf pattern would hold through stable weather but a pop-up thunderstorm could knock it sideways for a day before it reset. That's basically what happened. We had one squally afternoon roll through midweek, turned the surf off Fire Island a little sloppy and stained for about six hours, and the blues scattered off the beach front. By the next morning it had cleaned back up and the bunker schools were right back where they started, just off the bar at Kismet and working east toward Lonelyville.

Speaking of the blues — they are absolutely the story of the week, and I mean that in the best way. Cocktail blues, two to four pounds, some genuine choppers mixing in up to six or seven, and they're hammering everything from the beach out to a half mile. If you're surfcasting Fire Island at first light, white or bunker-colored Hopkins spoons and Ava jigs with a strip of pork rind are getting hit on nearly every retrieve when you find the bait balls. From the boat, same story off Democrat Point and along the outside of the inlet bar — troll a small spoon or cast poppers into the surface commotion when the birds start diving, and you'll load the box fast. This is the wave Mother Nature owed us after a slow June, and it's holding as long as that warm surface layer stays put.

Fluke are still the steady paycheck, and honestly this bite hasn't changed much in three weeks, which is a good thing. We flagged this pattern last week too — keepers mixed with shorts, steady rather than a blitz, and that's exactly what's showing up on the drift. The Robert Moses bridges, both the east and west spans, are producing fluke to five and six pounds in 25 to 35 feet of water on the tail end of the outgoing tide, when the current is still moving enough to keep your bucktail ticking bottom but hasn't gone full slack. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of fluke belly or squid, dragged slow along the channel edges — that's the program. Inside the bay, the flats off Nicoll Bay and around the Sexton Island cuts near Sayville are holding shorts mostly, but there are enough 19- and 20-inch fish mixed in to make it worth a few drifts before you run out to the bridges for the bigger stuff.

Great South Bay itself has been quiet on the striper front during daylight — too warm, too much boat traffic, too much sun on the flats. But work the deeper holes off Patchogue and the channel edges near Fire Island Inlet after dark, live eels or fresh bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, and there are still real bass in there, some pushing into the high 20s and low 30s. The tide matters here more than almost anything else this time of year — I want the first two hours of the incoming after sunset, when the cooler bay water starts pushing back in against that warm outgoing layer and creates just enough of a temperature edge to get the bigger fish moving and feeding.

Porgies and blackfish are still mostly a summer afterthought right now — there's a decent porgy bite on the reefs and rock piles off Fire Island Inlet on green crab and clam, but nobody's targeting them seriously with the blues and fluke this active. Weakfish have been scarce; a few reports of incidental fish mixed in with the fluke catch on the bay flats, but nothing like a dedicated bite worth chasing yet.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon, and that means stronger tides are coming by the weekend. Bigger swings usually stir the water column and can jolt the bass out of that strict nocturnal pattern, especially if we get any overnight cooling. If the wind stays out of the south and southwest and the surface holds warm, I'd keep playing the same hand — blues and fluke during the day, bass after dark. But if we catch a cold front behind one of these afternoon storms, don't be surprised if the daytime bass bite wakes back up at the inlet seam on the first hour of the incoming. That's the window I'll be watching closest, and where I'd have my rod rigged and ready if I only had one trip this week.
